Reference: Feger, Pavanini and Radulescu (2022)

Demand

We assume that household iii in year ttt maximises its utility from consuming electricity CitC_{it}Cit​ and the outside good QitQ_{it}Qit​, subject to a budget constraint. Household's constrained optimization problem:

max⁡C,Q  u(C,Q,X)s.t.PC+Q+F≤I−T(I)(8.1.2.1)\mathop{\max}_{C,Q}\;u(C,Q,X)\quad \text{s.t.}\quad PC+Q+F\leq I-T(I) \tag{8.1.2.1}maxC,Q​u(C,Q,X)s.t.PC+Q+F≤I−T(I)(8.1.2.1)

where III and XXX are respectively household's income and other characteristics (e.g., wealth, size, etc.), T(I)T(I)T(I) are income taxes, PPP is the energy price, and FFF is the fixed fee. We normalize the price of the outside good to 1. We define the following functional form for households' utility:

u(C,Q,X)=Q+ββ+1Cβ+1βeX′ω+ν−β(8.1.2.2)u(C,Q,X)=Q+\frac{\beta}{\beta+1}C^{\frac{\beta+1}{\beta}}e^{\frac{X'\omega+\nu}{-\beta}} \tag{8.1.2.2}u(C,Q,X)=Q+β+1β​Cββ+1​e−βX′ω+ν​(8.1.2.2)

The first order conditions lead us to the following energy demand function (C∗C^*C∗) and optimal consumption of the outside good (Q∗Q^*Q∗):

C∗=PβeX′ω+ν(8.1.2.3)C^*=P^{\beta}e^{X'\omega+\nu} \tag{8.1.2.3}C∗=PβeX′ω+ν(8.1.2.3)
Q∗=I~−Pβ+1eX′ω+ν(8.1.2.4)Q^*=\tilde{I}-P^{\beta+1}e^{X'\omega+\nu} \tag{8.1.2.4}Q∗=I~−Pβ+1eX′ω+ν(8.1.2.4)

where I~=I−T(I)\tilde{I}=I-T(I)I~=I−T(I) is income net of tax payments. Accordingly, the indirect utility function can be expressed as:

v(P,I~,X)=I~−1β+1Pβ+1eX′ω+ν=I~−1β+1PC∗(8.1.2.5)v(P,\tilde{I},X)=\tilde{I}-\frac{1}{\beta+1}P^{\beta+1}e^{X'\omega+\nu}=\tilde{I}-\frac{1}{\beta+1}PC^* \tag{8.1.2.5}v(P,I~,X)=I~−β+11​Pβ+1eX′ω+ν=I~−β+11​PC∗(8.1.2.5)

Now let's go to the energy demand function:

Cit(Λ)=Putβieα+Xit′ω+νit(8.1.2.6)C_{it}(\Lambda)=P_{ut}^{\beta_i}e^{\alpha+X^{'}_{it}\omega+\nu_{it}} \tag{8.1.2.6}Cit​(Λ)=Putβi​​eα+Xit′​ω+νit​(8.1.2.6)

where PutP_{ut}Put​ is the electricity marginal price charged by energy utility u∈{BKW,EWB,ET}u\in \{BKW,EWB,ET\}u∈{BKW,EWB,ET} in year ttt, XitX_{it}Xit​ are household and building characteristics that are likely to determine energy consumption, such as household size, home ownership, electric and water heating, house surface, and number of rooms. νit\nu_{it}νit​ are shocks to energy demand independently distributed across years and households, and Λ={α,βi,ω}\Lambda=\{\alpha,\beta_i,\omega\}Λ={α,βi​,ω} are the parameters of the demand function that we want to recover. We allow the price elasticity of demand βi\beta_iβi​ to vary across the quintiles of the wealth distribution, to capture any heterogeneity in price sensitivity across wealth groups. Since wealth is a stock variable, we view it as a more robust measure than income to capture differences in households' preferences. We use the estimates of the price elasticity βi\beta_iβi​ of energy consumption as well as observed consumption to compute the indirect utility of each household without a PV in year ttt⁠:

vit(PVit=0,Λ^)=I~−Fut−1β^i+1PutCit(8.1.2.7)v_{it}(\mathcal{PV}_{it}=0,\hat{\Lambda})=\tilde{I}-F_{ut}-\frac{1}{\hat{\beta}_i+1}P_{ut}C_{it} \tag{8.1.2.7}vit​(PVit​=0,Λ^)=I~−Fut​−β^​i​+11​Put​Cit​(8.1.2.7)

where I~it=Iit−T(Iit)\tilde{I}_{it}=I_{it}-T(I_{it})I~it​=Iit​−T(Iit​) is income net of income tax payments, and FutF_{ut}Fut​ is the fixed fee charged by energy utility uuu in year ttt⁠. A household that has installed a solar panel receives as additional utility the annual revenue generated by its solar panel Rit\mathcal{R}_{it}Rit​:

vit(PVit=1,Λ^)=I~−Fut−1β^i+1PutCit+Rit(8.1.2.8)v_{it}(\mathcal{PV}_{it}=1,\hat{\Lambda})=\tilde{I}-F_{ut}-\frac{1}{\hat{\beta}_i+1}P_{ut}C_{it}+\mathcal{R}_{it} \tag{8.1.2.8}vit​(PVit​=1,Λ^)=I~−Fut​−β^​i​+11​Put​Cit​+Rit​(8.1.2.8)

PV Revenue

Under a subsidized feed-in scheme, the revenue would be:

RitFT=∑s=tt+24ρs−t(1−ζ)s−t⋅τit⋅Yi⏟Feed-in Period+ρ25Rt+25SC⏟Post Feed-in period(8.1.2.9)\mathcal{R}_{it}^{FT}=\underbrace{\sum_{s=t}^{t+24}\rho^{s-t}(1-\zeta)^{s-t}\cdot \tau_{it}\cdot Y_i}_{\text{Feed-in Period}}+\underbrace{\rho^{25}\mathcal{R}_{t+25}^{SC}}_{\text{Post Feed-in period}} \tag{8.1.2.9}RitFT​=Feed-in Periods=t∑t+24​ρs−t(1−ζ)s−t⋅τit​⋅Yi​​​+Post Feed-in periodρ25Rt+25SC​​​(8.1.2.9)

where ρ\rhoρ is the discount factor, and ζ\zetaζ is the panel's degrade factor. Rt+25SC\mathcal{R}_{t+25}^{SC}Rt+25SC​ is the net present value of all additional PV revenue after the feed-in period. Note that the remuneration rate τit\tau_{it}τit​ is set at the time of installation and is fixed for the next 25 years.

In a self-consumption setting, a household has the incentive to directly consume its produced electricity. For each kWh a household directly consumes, it saves on the total electricity price PutP_{ut}Put​. The remaining produced electricity is fed into the grid and remunerated by the energy utility at electricity procurement price PuteP_{ut}^ePute​⁠, which is roughly half the total electricity price, the difference being comprised of the marginal grid price and taxes. Each household can directly consume a fixed share SCi\mathcal{SC}_{i}SCi​ of its electricity production YiY_iYi​, calculated by Eturnity as a function of the household's average level of electricity consumption, its appliances, and the total production of the PV. The total revenue under a self-consumption scenario reads as:

RitSC=∑s=t∞ρs−t(1−ζ)s−t⋅Yi⋅[SCi⋅E[Put]+(1−SCi)⋅E[Pute]](8.1.2.10)\mathcal{R}_{it}^{SC}=\sum_{s=t}^{\infty}\rho^{s-t}(1-\zeta)^{s-t}\cdot Y_i\cdot \left[ \mathcal{SC}_{i}\cdot E[P_{ut}]+(1-\mathcal{SC}_{i})\cdot E[P_{ut}^e] \right] \tag{8.1.2.10}RitSC​=s=t∑∞​ρs−t(1−ζ)s−t⋅Yi​⋅[SCi​⋅E[Put​]+(1−SCi​)⋅E[Pute​]](8.1.2.10)

Dynamic PV Adoption

We define the PV adoption decision as a Bellman equation, using as inputs the static consumption decision of household iii in each year ttt:

Vi(Sit)=max⁡PVit{θvvit(PVit)+εit(PVit)+PVit(θvVit+θFiFit)+(1−PVit)ρE[Vi(Sit+1) ∣ Sit]}(8.1.2.11)\begin{aligned} V_i(S_{it})&=\mathop{\max}_{\mathcal{PV}_{it}}\{\theta_vv_{it}(\mathcal{PV}_{it})+\varepsilon_{it}(\mathcal{PV}_{it})+\mathcal{PV}_{it}(\theta_vV_{it}+\theta_{Fi}\mathcal{F}_{it})+(1-\mathcal{PV}_{it})\rho E\left[V_i(S_{it+1})\,|\,S_{it}\right]\} \end{aligned} \tag{8.1.2.11}Vi​(Sit​)​=maxPVit​​{θv​vit​(PVit​)+εit​(PVit​)+PVit​(θv​Vit​+θFi​Fit​)+(1−PVit​)ρE[Vi​(Sit+1​)∣Sit​]}​(8.1.2.11)

where SitS_{it}Sit​ are the state variables of the dynamic problem, namely the total expected discounted value of PV revenue Rit\mathcal{R}_{it}Rit​ and the installation cost Fit\mathcal{F}_{it}Fit​⁠, and εit(PVit)\varepsilon_{it}(\mathcal{PV}_{it})εit​(PVit​) are independently and identically distributed type I extreme value shocks to the solar panel adoption choice, a state variable unobserved by the econometrician.

We define Vit=E[∑s=t+1∞ρs−tvis(1)]V_{it}=E\left[\sum_{s=t+1}^{\infty}\rho^{s-t}v_{is}(1)\right]Vit​=E[∑s=t+1∞​ρs−tvis​(1)] as the present discounted indirect utility under PV adoption for all future years. The parameter θFi\theta_{Fi}θFi​ measures households’ sensitivity to solar panel installation costs Fit\mathcal{F}_{it}Fit​⁠, and similarly to the energy demand model is heterogenous across households' wealth quintiles, while θv\theta_vθv​ scales the indirect utility, allowing for flexibility in the variance of εit(PVit)\varepsilon_{it}(\mathcal{PV}_{it})εit​(PVit​). In estimating equation (11), we aim to recover Θ={θv,θFi}\Theta=\{\theta_v,\theta_{Fi}\}Θ={θv​,θFi​}, since these capture the relative weight of the indirect utility from electricity consumption and of the fixed installation cost in households' adoption decisions.

The disutility of adopting a PV is a linear function of the fixed installation cost FitF_{it}Fit​⁠. Based on data availability, we construct gross fixed installation cost as:

Fit=(1−Ti)⋅kWpi⋅CtkWp(8.1.2.12)F_{it}=(1-T_i)\cdot kWp_i\cdot \mathcal{C}_t^{kWp} \tag{8.1.2.12}Fit​=(1−Ti​)⋅kWpi​⋅CtkWp​(8.1.2.12)

where kWpikWp_ikWpi​ is the size of the solar panel in kilowatt peak, which Eturnity simulated for us as a function of the roof size of the dwelling, CtkWp\mathcal{C}_t^{kWp}CtkWp​ is the installation cost per kilowatt peak, and TiT_iTi​ is the household's marginal income tax. In 2014, the Swiss regulator switched from a subsidized feed-in tariff to a lump sum subsidy equivalent to 30% of the installation cost. This further reduced the fixed installation cost to Fit=(1−S)(1−Ti)⋅kWpi⋅CtkWpF_{it}=(1-S)(1-T_i)\cdot kWp_i\cdot \mathcal{C}_t^{kWp}Fit​=(1−S)(1−Ti​)⋅kWpi​⋅CtkWp​, where SSS is the subsidy as share of installation costs. In the estimation, we include the subsidy for all observations in 2014.

Under conditional independence, we can write the following alternative specific expected value functions, describing a non-regenerative optimal stopping problem:

EVi(Sit,PVit)={θvvit(1)+θvVit+θFiFit,if PVit=1θvvit(0)+ρ∫Sit+1EVi(Sit+1)p1(Sit+1∣Sit,δ^),if PVit=0(8.1.2.13)EV_i(S_{it},PV_{it})=\begin{cases} \theta_vv_{it}(1)+\theta_vV_{it}+\theta_{Fi}F_{it},\quad \text{if }PV_{it}=1 \\ \theta_vv_{it}(0)+\rho \int_{S_{it+1}}EV_i(S_{it+1})p_1(S_{it+1}|S_{it},\hat{\delta}),\quad \text{if }PV_{it}=0 \end{cases} \tag{8.1.2.13}EVi​(Sit​,PVit​)={θv​vit​(1)+θv​Vit​+θFi​Fit​,if PVit​=1θv​vit​(0)+ρ∫Sit+1​​EVi​(Sit+1​)p1​(Sit+1​∣Sit​,δ^),if PVit​=0​(8.1.2.13)

where p1(Sit+1∣Sit,δ^)p_1(S_{it+1}|S_{it},\hat{\delta})p1​(Sit+1​∣Sit​,δ^) summarizes the transition probabilities of the state variables. We assume that households form expectations over the two aggregate variables in equation (9), the total PV revenue RitR_{it}Rit​ and the installation cost FitF_{it}Fit​⁠, as opposed to keeping track of all the variables that determine RitR_{it}Rit​⁠.

Transition Probabilities

We define the transition probabilities of the state variables Sit={Rit,Fit}S_{it}=\{R_{it},F_{it}\}Sit​={Rit​,Fit​} with an autoregressive process of order one for each. We further distinguish between two different processes for RitR_{it}Rit​ depending on the institutional setting in year ttt⁠, that could be feed-in tariff FTFTFT or self-consumption SCSCSC. While in the FTFTFT setting, the evolution of revenue is driven by the decline in feed-in tariffs, whereas in the SCSCSC setting, the evolution of revenue is driven by overall electricity prices. The estimated parameters of the processes δ^={δ^FT,δ^SC,δ^F}\hat{\delta}=\{\hat{\delta}_{FT},\hat{\delta}_{SC},\hat{\delta}_F\}δ^={δ^FT​,δ^SC​,δ^F​} act as inputs to construct the transition matrix for the dynamic part of the model. As is standard in the literature, we assume conditional independence between state variables observed by the econometrician SitS_{it}Sit​ and those unobserved by the econometrician εit\varepsilon_{it}εit​. In practice, we specify the following AR(1) processes:

RitFT=δFTRit−1FT+ηitFT,  ηitFT∼N(0,σFT)(8.1.2.16)R_{it}^{FT}=\delta_{FT}R_{it-1}^{FT}+\eta_{it}^{FT},\; \eta_{it}^{FT}\sim N(0,\sigma_{FT}) \tag{8.1.2.16}RitFT​=δFT​Rit−1FT​+ηitFT​,ηitFT​∼N(0,σFT​)(8.1.2.16)
RitSC=δSCRit−1SC+ηitSC,  ηitSC∼N(0,σSC)(8.1.2.17)R_{it}^{SC}=\delta_{SC}R_{it-1}^{SC}+\eta_{it}^{SC},\; \eta_{it}^{SC}\sim N(0,\sigma_{SC}) \tag{8.1.2.17}RitSC​=δSC​Rit−1SC​+ηitSC​,ηitSC​∼N(0,σSC​)(8.1.2.17)
Fit=δFFit−1+ηitF,  ηitF∼N(0,σF)(8.1.2.18)F_{it}=\delta_FF_{it-1}+\eta_{it}^F,\; \eta_{it}^{F}\sim N(0,\sigma_{F}) \tag{8.1.2.18}Fit​=δF​Fit−1​+ηitF​,ηitF​∼N(0,σF​)(8.1.2.18)

Estimation

The energy demand part of the model is estimated to recover the parameters Λ={α,βi,ω}\Lambda=\{\alpha,\beta_i,\omega\}Λ={α,βi​,ω}. The limited price variation over time and the small number of utilities in the sample represent a challenge for the identification of the price elasticity of demand βi\beta_iβi​⁠, a key parameter to capture the reaction of household consumption to changes in tariffs. The paper estimates the following regression model:

ln⁡(Cit)=α+βiln⁡(Put)+Xit′ω+μt+νˉit⏟νit(8.1.2.19)\ln (C_{it})=\alpha+\beta_i\ln(P_{ut})+X_{it}^{\prime}\omega+\underbrace{\mu_t+\bar{\nu}_{it}}_{\nu_{it}} \tag{8.1.2.19}ln(Cit​)=α+βi​ln(Put​)+Xit′​ω+νit​μt​+νˉit​​​(8.1.2.19)

In the dynamic PV adoption part of the model, the parameters of interest Θ={θv,θFi}\Theta=\{\theta_v,\theta_{Fi}\}Θ={θv​,θFi​} describe the impact on PV adoption of the indirect utility from PV revenue and of the fixed installation cost. We can recover the parameters that maximize the following log-likelihood function:

L(Θ)=∑i∑tlog⁡[Pr(PVit∣Sit;Θ)](8.1.2.20)L(\Theta)=\sum_i\sum_t\log \left[\text{Pr}(PV_{it}|S_{it};\Theta)\right] \tag{8.1.2.20}L(Θ)=i∑​t∑​log[Pr(PVit​∣Sit​;Θ)](8.1.2.20)

References

  • Feger, Fabian, Nicola Pavanini, and Doina Radulescu. 2022. “Welfare and redistribution in residential electricity markets with solar power.” The Review of Economic Studies, 89(6): 3267–3302.

This is the household's static problem, solved separately in every year. The choice variables are electricity consumption CCC (kWh per year) and a composite outside good QQQ whose price is normalised to one, so that QQQ is measured in money. The left-hand side of the constraint is total spending: the variable part of the electricity bill PCPCPC, where PPP is the marginal price per kWh, plus the outside good, plus the fixed fee FFF that the utility charges whatever the level of consumption. The right-hand side is disposable income I~=I−T(I)\tilde{I}=I-T(I)I~=I−T(I). The tariff is therefore a two-part tariff, linear in CCC with intercept FFF.

Because the utility function in equation (2) is strictly increasing in QQQ, the constraint binds, and the problem collapses to a one-dimensional choice of CCC:

max⁡C  u(C,  I~−F−PC,  X)\max_{C}\; u\big(C,\;\tilde{I}-F-PC,\;X\big)Cmax​u(C,I~−F−PC,X)

Two features matter later. First, FFF and T(I)T(I)T(I) enter only through the budget. With the quasi-linear utility of equation (2) they are pure transfers: they move welfare one for one but leave CCC unchanged, which is what allows the paper to study redistribution through fixed fees and taxes separately from the consumption distortion created by PPP. Second, the problem is static. A solar panel enters only as an addition to income, as in equation (8), and the adoption decision is layered on top of it in equation (11). The solution is given in equations (3) and (4), and the maximised value in equation (5).

Utility is quasi-linear: linear in the outside good QQQ and concave in electricity CCC. Quasi-linearity removes income effects, so electricity demand depends only on the price and on the taste shifter X′ω+νX'\omega+\nuX′ω+ν, and utility is measured in money, so indirect utilities can be compared and added across households in the welfare analysis. The shifter collects observed household and building characteristics XXX and an unobserved shock ν\nuν; the parameter β<0\beta<0β<0 turns out to be the price elasticity of demand.

The exponent on CCC is β+1β\frac{\beta+1}{\beta}ββ+1​, the reciprocal of the coefficient ββ+1\frac{\beta}{\beta+1}β+1β​. This is the functional form that generates equations (3), (4) and (5):

u(C,Q,X)=Q+ββ+1Cβ+1βeX′ω+ν−βu(C,Q,X)=Q+\frac{\beta}{\beta+1}C^{\frac{\beta+1}{\beta}}e^{\frac{X'\omega+\nu}{-\beta}}u(C,Q,X)=Q+β+1β​Cββ+1​e−βX′ω+ν​

It is what one obtains by integrating the inverse demand implied by equation (3). Writing A≡eX′ω+νA\equiv e^{X'\omega+\nu}A≡eX′ω+ν, demand C=PβAC=P^{\beta}AC=PβA gives the inverse demand P=(C/A)1/βP=(C/A)^{1/\beta}P=(C/A)1/β, and

This defines the expected discounted revenue from a panel installed in year ttt under the subsidised feed-in tariff regime. There is no uncertainty in this term, which is what makes a feed-in tariff attractive to a household. After 25 years the contract ends and the household moves to the self-consumption regime; Rt+25SC\mathcal{R}_{t+25}^{SC}Rt+25SC​ is the value, as of year t+25t+25t+25, of all later revenue, computed as in equation (10), and ρ25\rho^{25}ρ25 discounts it to year ttt.

This defines the expected discounted revenue of a panel under the self-consumption regime, in which there is no guaranteed tariff. Annual production (1−ζ)s−tYi(1-\zeta)^{s-t}Y_i(1−ζ)s−tYi​ is split into two parts. A share SCi\mathcal{SC}_{i}SCi​ is consumed directly in the home; each such kWh replaces a purchase from the grid and is therefore worth the full retail price PutP_{ut}Put​. The remaining share 1−SCi1-\mathcal{SC}_{i}1−SCi​ is fed into the grid and paid the procurement (energy-only) price PuteP_{ut}^ePute​, which is roughly half of the retail price because it excludes grid charges and taxes. The term in brackets is thus the expected value of one kWh produced, a weighted average of the two prices that always lies between E[Pute]E[P_{ut}^e]E[Pute​] and E[Put]E[P_{ut}]E[Put​] and increases with the self-consumption share. The share SCi\mathcal{SC}_{i}SCi​ is treated as a fixed, household-specific number computed by Eturnity; it is not a choice variable.

The sum runs to infinity, so the panel is assumed to last forever, with output shrinking at rate ζ\zetaζ. As written, the expected prices carry the subscript ttt and not sss, so the bracket does not depend on sss and the series is geometric with ratio q≡ρ(1−ζ)q\equiv\rho(1-\zeta)q≡ρ(1−ζ):

A kWh is worth 0.13 francs, annual revenue is 1300 francs, q=0.94525q=0.94525q=0.94525, and RitSC\mathcal{R}_{it}^{SC}RitSC​ is about 23700 francs. This Bellman equation defines the dynamic adoption problem as an optimal stopping problem. Each year a household without a panel chooses PVit∈{0,1}\mathcal{PV}_{it}\in\{0,1\}PVit​∈{0,1}. The ratio θFi/θv\theta_{Fi}/\theta_vθFi​/θv​ measures how a franc of upfront cost is weighted against a franc of discounted revenue. This constructs the installation cost state variable from the available data. The size of the panel kWpikWp_ikWpi​, in kilowatt peak, is the capacity that Eturnity simulated for each dwelling from its roof area; it is a fixed characteristic of household iii and not a choice. The price CtkWp\mathcal{C}_t^{kWp}CtkWp​ is the cost of installing one kilowatt peak in year ttt, which is common to all households and falls over time. Their product is the pre-tax cost of the installation. The factor (1−Ti)(1-T_i)(1−Ti​), where TiT_iTi​ is the household's marginal income tax rate, reflects the fact that installation costs can be deducted from taxable income, so each franc spent costs the household only 1−Ti1-T_i1−Ti​ francs after tax. The deduction is worth more to households with high marginal tax rates, which is one of the regressive elements of solar policy that the paper studies.

This is the law of motion that households are assumed to use to forecast the revenue state variable under the feed-in tariff regime. RitFTR_{it}^{FT}RitFT​ is the discounted revenue from equation (9) that a household would obtain by installing in year ttt; it changes from year to year mainly because the regulator lowers the tariff τit\tau_{it}τit​ offered to new installations. The coefficient δFT\delta_{FT}δFT​ is the persistence of the process, and ηitFT\eta_{it}^{FT}ηitFT​ is a normal innovation with dispersion σFT\sigma_{FT}σFT​ (the notation does not say whether this is the variance or the standard deviation). There is no intercept, so the forecast is proportional:

E[Rit+kFT ∣ RitFT]=δFTkRitFTE\left[R_{it+k}^{FT}\,|\,R_{it}^{FT}\right]=\delta_{FT}^{k}R_{it}^{FT}E[Rit+kFT​∣RitFT​]=δFTk​RitFT​

A value δFT<1\delta_{FT}<1δFT​<1 means that households expect the revenue from installing later to shrink geometrically, which lowers the value of waiting in equation (14) and pushes adoption forward.

The process implies the conditional density Rit+1FT ∣ RitFT∼N(δFTRitFT,σFT)R_{it+1}^{FT}\,|\,R_{it}^{FT}\sim N(\delta_{FT}R_{it}^{FT},\sigma_{FT})Rit+1FT​∣RitFT​∼N(δFT​RitFT​,σFT​), which is the revenue part of p1(Sit+1∣Sit,δ^)p_1(S_{it+1}|S_{it},\hat{\delta})p1​(Sit+1​∣Sit​,δ^) in equations (13) to (15); in practice it is discretised on a grid to form a transition matrix. The parameters are estimated in a first stage, outside the dynamic model, by regressing revenue on its own lag, and are then held fixed. The specification is a reduced-form description of beliefs: households track the single aggregate RitR_{it}Rit​ and not the tariff, prices and production that determine it, which keeps the state space two-dimensional. The persistence is identified from the year-to-year co-movement of computed revenue within households during the feed-in years.

This is the counterpart of equation (16) for the self-consumption regime. RitSCR_{it}^{SC}RitSC​ is the discounted revenue from equation (10) for a panel installed in year ttt. Under self-consumption there is no administratively set tariff, so revenue moves with the retail price PutP_{ut}Put​ and the procurement price PuteP_{ut}^ePute​, weighted by the self-consumption share. The coefficient δSC\delta_{SC}δSC​ therefore captures the persistence, and any trend, of electricity prices as they translate into revenue, and ηitSC\eta_{it}^{SC}ηitSC​ is a normal innovation with dispersion σSC\sigma_{SC}σSC​. The kkk-step forecast is

E[Rit+kSC ∣ RitSC]=δSCkRitSCE\left[R_{it+k}^{SC}\,|\,R_{it}^{SC}\right]=\delta_{SC}^{k}R_{it}^{SC}E[Rit+kSC​∣RitSC​]=δSCk​RitSC​

so δSC\delta_{SC}δSC​ close to one means that current revenue is expected to persist, while δSC>1\delta_{SC}>1δSC​>1 would mean that households expect revenue to grow, which makes waiting less costly.

A separate process is specified for each regime because the driving forces differ: a policy-determined decline in tariffs in one case, market and regulated electricity prices in the other. Which process applies depends on the institutional setting in year ttt, and households are assumed to forecast with the process of the prevailing regime. The implied conditional density N(δSCRitSC,σSC)N(\delta_{SC}R_{it}^{SC},\sigma_{SC})N(δSC​RitSC​,σSC​) is the revenue part of p1(Sit+1∣Sit,δ^)p_1(S_{it+1}|S_{it},\hat{\delta})p1​(Sit+1​∣Sit​,δ^) in the self-consumption years. As in equation (16), the parameters are estimated in a first stage from the within-household time variation of computed revenue, there is no intercept, and the innovation is assumed independent of the adoption shocks εit\varepsilon_{it}εit​.

This is the law of motion for the second state variable, the installation cost FitF_{it}Fit​ of equation (12). Since panel size and the tax rate are fixed for a household, the time variation in FitF_{it}Fit​ comes from the cost per kilowatt peak CtkWp\mathcal{C}_t^{kWp}CtkWp​, which fell steadily over the sample, and from the introduction of the investment subsidy. The coefficient δF\delta_FδF​ summarises this trend, and ηitF\eta_{it}^{F}ηitF​ is a normal innovation with dispersion σF\sigma_FσF​. The forecast is

E[Fit+k ∣ Fit]=δFkFitE\left[F_{it+k}\,|\,F_{it}\right]=\delta_F^{k}F_{it}E[Fit+k​∣Fit​]=δFk​Fit​

With δF<1\delta_F<1δF​<1 households expect installation to become cheaper every year. This is the main source of option value in the model: by equation (14), waiting one year postpones revenue but lowers the expected cost by the factor δF\delta_FδF​, weighted by θFi\theta_{Fi}θFi​. For instance, with δF=0.9\delta_F=0.9δF​=0.9 a cost of 20000 francs is expected to be 18000 francs next year and 16200 francs the year after.

Together with equation (16) or equation (17), this process defines the transition density of the state. The two innovations are specified separately, so the density factorises:

p1(Sit+1∣Sit,δ^)=p(Rit+1∣Rit,δ^)⋅p(Fit+1∣Fit,δ^F)p_1(S_{it+1}|S_{it},\hat{\delta})=p(R_{it+1}|R_{it},\hat{\delta})\cdot p(F_{it+1}|F_{it},\hat{\delta}_F)p1​(Sit+1​∣Sit​,δ^)=p(Rit+1​∣Rit​,δ^)⋅p(Fit+1​∣Fit​,δ^F​)

As for the revenue processes, δF\delta_FδF​ and σF\sigma_FσF​ are estimated in a first stage by regressing cost on its lag and are then treated as known when the dynamic problem is solved. Because the cost per kilowatt peak is common to all households, the persistence is identified essentially from the aggregate time path of costs, and the proportional form means that the expected franc decline is larger for households with large roofs.

This is the estimating equation for the demand parameters Λ={α,βi,ω}\Lambda=\{\alpha,\beta_i,\omega\}Λ={α,βi​,ω}. It is the logarithm of the demand function in equation (6),

ln⁡Cit=ln⁡(Putβieα+Xit′ω+νit)=α+βiln⁡Put+Xit′ω+νit\ln C_{it}=\ln\left(P_{ut}^{\beta_i}e^{\alpha+X_{it}'\omega+\nu_{it}}\right)=\alpha+\beta_i\ln P_{ut}+X_{it}'\omega+\nu_{it}lnCit​=ln(Putβi​​eα+Xit′​ω+νit​)=α+βi​lnPut​+Xit′​ω+νit​

with the demand shock decomposed as νit=μt+νˉit\nu_{it}=\mu_t+\bar{\nu}_{it}νit​=μt​+νˉit​. The year effect μt\mu_tμt​ absorbs everything that shifts consumption of all households in a given year, such as weather or aggregate economic conditions, and νˉit\bar{\nu}_{it}νˉit​ is the idiosyncratic error. The dependent variable is annual consumption in logs, and the coefficient on the log marginal price is the elasticity βi\beta_iβi​, estimated separately for each wealth quintile, in practice by interacting ln⁡Put\ln P_{ut}lnPut​ with quintile indicators. The vector ω\omegaω gives the semi-elasticities of consumption with respect to the characteristics in XitX_{it}Xit​.

Identification of βi\beta_iβi​ is demanding. The price varies only at the level of the utility and the year, there are three utilities, and the year effects remove common movements in prices. What remains is differential changes in tariffs across utilities over time, together with cross-sectional price differences that are not captured by XitX_{it}Xit​. Consistency requires that νˉit\bar{\nu}_{it}νˉit​ is uncorrelated with ln⁡Put\ln P_{ut}lnPut​ conditional on XitX_{it}Xit​ and μt\mu_tμt​, which is plausible in so far as regulated tariffs are set from costs and not in response to household-level demand shocks. Because the tariff is linear with a fixed fee, the marginal price does not depend on the household's own consumption, so the simultaneity that arises with block tariffs is absent.

The estimate matters for welfare through equation (7), where the bill is scaled by 1β^i+1\frac{1}{\hat{\beta}_i+1}β^​i​+11​: with β^i=−0.2\hat{\beta}_i=-0.2β^​i​=−0.2 the factor is 1.25, with β^i=−0.5\hat{\beta}_i=-0.5β^​i​=−0.5 it is 2.

The second product involves only the transition parameters, which are estimated beforehand from equations (16) to (18). Holding them at δ^\hat{\delta}δ^, the part that depends on Θ\ThetaΘ is the first product. Each factor is a binary outcome whose probability comes from equation (15):

Households are independent, so the sample likelihood is the product over iii; taking logs turns the products into sums:

which is the target equation. Two points on how it is used. First, because adoption is an absorbing state, the sum over ttt for a household runs over the years in which it is still at risk, that is, up to and including the year of adoption; later years involve no decision and contribute nothing. Second, evaluating L(Θ)L(\Theta)L(Θ) requires the value of waiting in equation (15), so for each trial value of Θ\ThetaΘ the fixed point of equations (13) and (14) is solved, given δ^\hat{\delta}δ^, and the resulting probabilities are inserted; the outer search over Θ={θv,θFi}\Theta=\{\theta_v,\theta_{Fi}\}Θ={θv​,θFi​} maximises LLL. The parameter θv\theta_vθv​ is identified by how adoption responds to variation in RitR_{it}Rit​ across households and regimes, and θFi\theta_{Fi}θFi​ by the response to FitF_{it}Fit​ within each wealth quintile. The discount factor ρ\rhoρ is not estimated but fixed.
